summary: Black swallow-wort, also called black dog-strangling vine, is a climbing vine that forms large patches that grow over and smother native plants. Deer avoid eating it, and its tangled patches are hard to walk through. Monarch butterflies sometimes lay eggs on it, but the caterpillars cannot survive, and it can crowd out the milkweed monarchs need. Its small, star-shaped flowers are deep purple-black.
history: Black swallow-wort is native to the western Mediterranean region. It may first have been brought to North America as an ornamental plant.
seasons: Shoots come up in spring, the plants flower in early summer, and seed pods 1.5 to 3 inches long form in late July and early August. The seeds are carried by the wind, and a square meter of swallow-wort can produce 1,000 to 2,000 seeds a year.

handling.text: Its deep, fibrous roots make it hard to remove; if digging it up, get as much of the root crown as possible. For small patches, plants and seed pods can be bagged before they release seed. Mowing won't get rid of it, and mowing after seeds form can spread them. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
